articles.title: Silent Teachers in Anatomical Education: A Historical Review of Paradigm Shifts in Human Cadaver Procurement Since Ancient Persia.
articles.authors: Seyed Behnamedin Jameie, Setareh Nejadrostam, Melika Jameie et al.
articles.abstract: Human cadaveric dissection has played an important role in the development of anatomical knowledge and remains an established component of medical education. The availability of human bodies for anatomical study has varied across historical periods, reflecting changes in educational institutions, procurement practices, and ethical and sociocultural considerations. This narrative review examines the historical development of human dissection and cadaver procurement, with particular emphasis on Iran. Relevant literature was identified through searches of MEDLINE via PubMed and supplemented by historical publications, scholarly sources, locally sourced literature and contextual information, reference-list screening, and citation tracking. The literature was synthesized chronologically and thematically to examine the development of anatomical knowledge, the emergence of modern anatomy education in Iran, and reported changes in cadaver procurement practices. The historical literature documents a long tradition of medical scholarship and anatomical knowledge in Iran, followed by the gradual development of formal anatomy education through modern medical institutions. Reported sources of cadavers for anatomical education in Iran have included unclaimed bodies, imported cadavers, and voluntary body donation. However, the available evidence is insufficient to establish a comprehensive chronology of these practices or to determine their relative contributions across institutions and historical periods. The increasing recognition of voluntary body donation represents an important development in contemporary anatomical education, alongside continuing ethical and sociocultural considerations concerning informed consent, respect for human remains, and public acceptance. Cadaveric dissection continues to be used alongside alternative teaching approaches, including anatomical models and digital technologies. The historical development of cadaver procurement in Iran reflects broader changes in anatomical education and institutional practice. Further research based on historical records and institutional documentation is needed to clarify the chronology of procurement practices and their implications for contemporary anatomical education and ethical governance.

articles.title: A comprehensive review of craniomandibular morphometric indices in carnivora: Anatomical basis, functional significance, and comparative applications.
articles.authors: Babak Rasouli
articles.abstract: The skull of carnivorans represents a highly integrated anatomical structure shaped by selective pressures associated with feeding ecology, sensory specialization, locomotion, and phylogenetic history. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of craniomandibular morphometric indices in the order Carnivora, integrating their anatomical definitions, morphometric foundations, and functional significance. Standardized cranial and mandibular measurements are reviewed together with 11 widely used proportional indices, including the Cranial Index (CI), Skull Index (SI), Facial Index (FI), Facial Length Index (FLI), Cranial Length Index (CLI), Cranial Height Index (CHI), Orbital Index (OI), Palatal Index (PI), Foramen Magnum Index (FMI), Mandibular Body Index (MBI), and Mandibular Ramus Index (MRI). The review highlights the biomechanical and evolutionary relevance of these indices by examining their relationships with bite performance, craniofacial organization, sensory adaptations, feeding ecology, and morphological diversification among carnivoran families. In addition to summarizing published morphometric indices, several proportional indices that have rarely been reported as independent variables are derived from previously published linear craniometric measurements, providing standardized quantitative descriptors for comparative analyses across species. By compiling anatomical landmarks, measurement protocols, functional interpretations, and comparative data within a unified framework, this review identifies current knowledge gaps and promotes greater methodological consistency in future studies. Although some proportional indices were calculated from published measurements rather than directly reported in the original literature, they provide valuable complementary metrics for evaluating cranial and mandibular morphology. Overall, the integration of these 11 morphometric indices offers a comprehensive approach for investigating craniofacial evolution, functional morphology, feeding adaptations, and taxonomic diversity in both extant and fossil carnivorans. This review provides a practical reference for researchers in comparative anatomy, evolutionary biology, paleontology, and veterinary morphology.

articles.title: Paleontological and paleoenvironmental analyses of the Barro Alto site: A window to the mid Permian of western Gondwana.
articles.authors: Douglas da Silva Strattmann, Amanda Goulart Rodrigues, Pedro Lucas de Barros Pruciano et al.
articles.abstract: The Barro Alto fossil site (Rio Grande do Sul State, Brazil) is considered a prolific place for understanding the Guadalupian (Wordian) vertebrate diversity, especially for tetrapods and cartilaginous fishes. However, its paleoenvironmental context has not been deeply discussed in the literature. The present work aims to integrate previous and new paleontological data for this fossiliferous site and provide the depositional context for the Permian fauna of the Rio do Rasto Formation (Paraná Basin) at the Barro Alto site. The stratigraphic columnar profile is divided into six sedimentary facies grouped into two facies associations, which were integrated with paleontological and petrological data. The association of facies suggests that the paleoenvironmental context for the Barro Alto fossil site consists of a lacustrine paleoenvironment with seasonal variations in water levels and sediment influx, being eventually invaded by river channels. Furthermore, it contained a remarkable diversity of vertebrate remains, with bony (both Actinopterygii and Sarcopterygii) and cartilaginous fishes, terrestrial tetrapods from different groups such as anomodont synapsids, archosauromorphs, and temnospondyls, besides coprolites and plant remains. Additionally, recent paleontological studies involving the Karoo basin in South Africa may suggest a geochronological repositioning of the Barro Alto site to the Wordian due to biostratigraphic relationships between South African and Brazilian taxa.

articles.title: Mechanistic investigation of central, coronary, and arterial hemodynamics during lower body negative pressure using a validated 0D-1D cardiovascular model.
articles.authors: Francesco Tripoli, Luca Ridolfi, Jerry J Batzel et al.
articles.abstract: Lower body negative pressure (LBNP) is used in physiological and space medicine research as a tool to simulate central hypovolemia and orthostatic loading. Despite its extensive application, hemodynamic characterization is fragmented due to limitations in current acquisition methodologies and substantial inter-individual variability in LBNP-induced cardiovascular responses. This study presents an advanced multiscale 0D-1D cardiovascular model to investigate the hemodynamic response to graded LBNP (0 to -50 mmHg). The model combines a 1D representation of the arterial and coronary trees with a 0D description of the peripheral, venous, cardiopulmonary, coronary, and cerebro-ocular circulations. The model accounts for short-term regulatory mechanisms (i.e., baroreflex, cardiopulmonary reflex, and cerebral autoregulation) and includes transcapillary fluid exchange and lymphatic return to the heart. Model outcomes were validated against in vivo measurements obtained during a previously published graded LBNP experimental study. Once validated, the model enabled a detailed investigation of cardiac and arterial hemodynamics, including ventricular mechano-energetic and oxygen consumption parameters, coronary circulation, and pressure wave propagation throughout the arterial tree. The simulations revealed a greater mechano-energetic vulnerability of the right ventricle compared with the left ventricle, whereas coronary blood flow remained nearly constant despite the increase in rate-pressure product at higher LBNP levels. Wave propagation analysis revealed variations limited to the lower-limb arteries due to elevated transmural pressure and arterial stiffening. The proposed in silico - in vivo framework provides a comprehensive description of cardiovascular responses to LBNP, offering mechanistic insights that are difficult to obtain experimentally.

articles.title: Neural Profiles of Pistol Shooting Performance Across Skill Levels in Hearing and Deaf Shooters: Insights into Cognitive-Motor Processes.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Ting-Yu Chueh, Jia-Hao Wu, Tsung-Min Hung et al.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Precision sport performance requires optimal motor preparation supported by efficient neural processing. While the psychomotor efficiency framework has been used to explain expertise-related neural patterns, it remains unclear whether such neural signatures generalize across individuals with different sensory experiences. The present study aimed to examine expertise-related neural oscillations during motor preparation in 10-m air-pistol shooting by comparing skilled and novice performers in hearing and deaf populations. METHODS: Study 1 included 37 hearing participants (skilled: n = 19; novice: n = 18), whereas Study 2 included 43 deaf participants (skilled: n = 19; novice: n = 24). Electroencephalography (EEG) was used to assess temporal alpha asymmetry (T4 minus T3), parietal alpha, occipital alpha, frontocentral alpha, sensorimotor rhythm (SMR), and frontal midline theta during the 4 s preceding trigger pull. RESULTS: In Study 1, skilled hearing shooters showed lower temporal alpha asymmetry, reflecting relatively greater left temporal alpha power. They also exhibited higher posterior and frontocentral alpha power, a time-specific increase in SMR, and higher frontal midline theta power relative to novice shooters. In contrast, Study 2 revealed a distinct neural profile in deaf shooters. Deaf novices showed a time-dependent decrease in temporal alpha asymmetry as the trigger pull approached, whereas skilled deaf shooters remained relatively stable. In addition, skilled deaf performers showed reduced frontocentral alpha and SMR power relative to novices, indicating greater sensorimotor cortical engagement during motor preparation. CONCLUSIONA: These findings highlight population specificity in expertise-related neural profiles, indicating that neural markers of expertise may not generalize across sensory contexts. Rather than reflecting a universal pattern of psychomotor efficiency, the observed neural profiles may vary across populations with different sensory experiences. Overall, the present study highlights the importance of considering sensory experience when examining neural optimization and provides insights into the cognitive-motor processes underlying skilled performance across diverse athletic populations in precision sports.

articles.title: 3D Biomechanics of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries in Football: What We Have Learned in the Last Five Years.
articles.authors: Matteo Zago, Francesco Della Villa
articles.abstract: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture is among the most impacting injuries in professional football. Understanding these injuries in their environment, and their biomechanical mechanism, is the bottleneck between injury surveillance and effective mechanism-informed prevention and rehabilitation. We reconstructed the three-dimensional kinematics of 33 cases of ACL injury sustained by elite male football players during official matches. The Model-Based Image-Matching technique was leveraged to obtain quantitative, detailed estimates of three-dimensional joint kinematics, thereby overcoming the limitations of traditional bidimensional video analyses. This paper reviews and interprets findings derived from over five years of research on the topic from a novel perspective. At the knee level, ACL injury mechanics involved a sequence of multiplanar joint rotations; on the sagittal plane, knee flexion increased from initial contact to injury frame; on the frontal plane, a knee abduction (valgus) shift emerged; on the transverse plane, following ground contact, we observed a sequence of internal and then external rotation of the femur, relative to the tibia, occurring during loading acceptance. Expanding the analysis on total-body kinematics, marked inter-individual variability was observed across the studied cohort; while ACL failure exhibits consistent kinematic features at the knee level, the sequence of whole-body postures leading to injury appears to be context-dependent. Finally, we propose biomechanically informed approaches to injury mitigation, emphasizing the integration of sport-specific contextual determinants, perceptual and decision-making processes, challenging the traditional separation between technical coaching and injury prevention.

articles.title: Individualized Amplitude-Time Models of Post-activation Performance Enhancement Using the Velocity-Loss Method in Trained Populations: A Systematic Review and Individual Participant Data Meta-analysis.
articles.authors: Jun Li, Kai Xu, Yuming Zhong et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Five study-level models describe post-activation performance enhancement (PAPE) amplitude-time characteristics: (i) nil or fluctuating, (ii) immediate enhancement, (iii) inverted-U enhancement, (iv) skewed or delayed inverted-U enhancement, and (v) performance impairment. However, the moderators of these models at the individual level remain unclear. Velocity-loss (VL) approaches, which reflect neuromuscular fatigue, may provide a useful framework to better understand these amplitude-time characteristics. OBJECTIVES: The aims of this study were (i) to establish an individualized PAPE amplitude-time model using VL-based conditioning activities (CAs); (ii) to examine how relative maximal strength (RMS) affects performance changes across recovery times at the individual level; and (iii) to investigate how VL methods influence study-level PAPE amplitude-time characteristics through within- and between-study analyses. METHODS: Three databases were systematically searched. Studies were included if CA involved squats or bench presses prescribed using the VL method and reported performance outcomes reflecting PAPE magnitude. Individual performance-recovery relationships were modeled using linear and nonlinear regression. A generalized linear mixed-effects model was applied to analyze the one-stage (individual participant data) effects of RMS on performance changes, while a three-level (multilevel) model was used for two-stage (study-level) meta-analysis. Multivariate linear and nonlinear models tested moderators including recovery time, sex, CA type, VL threshold, %1-repetition maximum (RM), and number of sets. RESULTS: Fifteen studies were included, with individual data from nine studies (248 participants: 224 males, 24 females). Individual performance-recovery responses generally matched the five established study-level PAPE amplitude-time patterns, though random deviations were observed. One-stage analyses revealed that individuals with low RMS (< ~ 1.5, unstable estimates) exhibited early enhancement followed by decline, whereas those with high RMS (> ~ 1.5) showed early decrements followed by an inverted-U response. Greater RMS was linked to smaller peak improvements (β = - 2.65) but was unrelated to minimum values (β = - 0.86). In females, maximal improvements occurred at RMS ~ 1.00-1.25, with lowest minimum values at ~ 1.25-1.50. Two-stage analyses indicated that VL alone did not significantly improve performance (standardized mean change = 0.11), but yielded greater improvements than control conditions (rest or traditional CA; standardized mean difference = 0.35). Recovery time, %1-RM, and VL threshold emerged as key moderators. CONCLUSIONS: Individual PAPE amplitude-time models exhibited random deviations from, but generally reflected, study-level patterns. Strength level influenced individual responses, with distinct PAPE profiles observed across participants. At the study level, 5% VL, 10% VL, and 60-90% 1-RM CAs appeared most effective for inducing peak PAPE responses. However, at the individual level, there was no single 'optimal' prescription, only a 'most suitable' one. PROTOCOL REGISTRATION: The original protocol was prospectively registered ( osf.io/hf6px ) with the Open Science Framework.

articles.title: Presynaptic GluN2D containing NMDARs on CA1 Shaffer collateral terminals control the release of glutamate onto pyramidal cells.
articles.authors: Tue G Banke, Jean-Francois Pare, Viktor J Olah et al.
articles.abstract: NMDA receptors (NMDARs) are expressed throughout the brain and, in addition to their central role in synaptic transmission, are essential mediators of many forms of synaptic plasticity. Given their widespread expression, it is not surprising that NMDAR dysfunction has been implicated in numerous neurological and neuropsychiatric disorders, including epilepsy, autism spectrum disorders and depression. NMDARs are localized at both pre- and postsynaptic sites, but presynaptic NMDARs are poorly understood. Here, by combining the use of wild-type and NMDAR subunit-specific knockout mice, a series of highly selective subunit-specific pharmacological modulators, and electron microscopy analysis of immunostained brain sections, we describe GluN2D-containing NMDARs located presynaptically on CA3 pyramidal neuron axon terminals. We show that presynaptic NMDARs at the Schaffer collateral terminals control the probability of glutamate release onto connecting CA1 pyramidal neurons, but not Schaffer innervation of radiatum interneurons. Thus, GluN2D-containing NMDARs could be involved in various forms of plasticity. KEY POINTS: Functional presynaptic NMDA receptors (NMDARs) are present on CA3 pyramidal cell presynaptic terminals synapsing onto pyramidal cells Presynaptic NMDARs contain GluN2D and GluN2B subunits Activation of presynaptic GluN2D-containing NMDARs enhances the probability of vesicular release of glutamate Presynaptic GluN2D-containing NMDARs regulate short-term plasticity.

articles.title: Plasma Amino Acid Responses to an Oral Glucose Challenge Relate More Strongly to Obesity Than to Insulin Resistance.
articles.journal: American journal of physiology. Endocrinology and metabolism
articles.authors: Eduardo D S Freitas, Kailin A Johnson, Matthew Buras et al.
articles.abstract: The coexistence of obesity and insulin resistance is associated with elevated plasma amino acid concentrations. However, it remains unclear whether obesity or insulin resistance is more strongly associated with plasma amino acid dysregulation. Twenty-one adults were studied spanning a broad range of obesity and insulin resistance, and who underwent an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). Insulin resistance was assessed in the basal state using the homeostasis model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) and during the OGTT from the OGTT-derived plasma glucose and insulin responses, using the Matsuda insulin sensitivity index (Matsuda-ISI). Principal component analysis (PCA) revealed greater clustering of amino acid responses according to obesity-related measures (body mass index, body fat, body fat percentage, and waist circumference), as well as HOMA-IR and Matsuda-ISI, during the OGTT-stimulated state compared with the fasting state. Regression analyses showed statistically significant models (P < 0.05) only for branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs) in both the fasting and OGTT-stimulated states. The models explained 59% and 67% of the variance in BCAA outcomes in the fasting and OGTT-stimulated states, respectively. A composite obesity score, derived from the obesity-related measures, was a significant predictor of BCAAs in both states, whereas indices of insulin resistance/sensitivity were not. In conclusion, these exploratory findings show that plasma amino acids, specifically BCAAs, are more closely related to obesity than to insulin resistance, with these differences in plasma amino acid profiles becoming more evident during an OGTT-stimulated state than in the fasting state.

articles.title: A single bout of intermittent hypoxia provides an inhibitory control benefit across the continuum of low- to high-fit young adults.
articles.authors: Antonio Mendes, Nasimi A Guluzade, Emma D F X Miller et al.
articles.abstract: Exposure to brief alternating intervals of hypoxic and normoxic breathing (i.e., intermittent hypoxia: IH) increases cerebral blood flow (CBF) and is a change linked to a post-intervention executive function (EF) benefit. It is, however, unknown whether cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) influences the benefit. This is a salient question because individuals with higher CRF show increased CBF and more efficient dynamic cerebral autoregulation in response to environmental stressors - a change that may potentiate post-IH EF benefits. Here, healthy young adults classified as high-fit (n = 18: V ̇ O 2 peak range: 42-75 mL/kg/min) and low-fit (n = 18: V ̇ O 2 peak range: 13-35 mL/kg/min) completed a 60-min IH condition involving alternating 5-min intervals of hypoxic ( P ET O 2 = 50 mmHg) and normoxic (room air: P ET O 2 ≈ 90-95 mmHg) breathing (IH condition), and on a separate day completed a same duration normoxic control condition. During both conditions, participants' end-tidal carbon dioxide was maintained at a baseline level (i.e., normocapnic). Near-infrared spectroscopy and transcranial Doppler ultrasound measured cortical haemodynamics, and the antisaccade task was used to assess EF at baseline (T0), and at immediate (T1), and 30-min post-intervention (T2) timepoints. Results showed that high- and low-fit individuals produced an equivalent magnitude reduction in cortical oxygenation and increase in middle cerebral artery velocity (MCAv) during hypoxic intervals. Both groups produced an equivalent magnitude reduction in antisaccade reaction times at T2, and this benefit was unrelated to changes in cortical oxygenation or MCAv. Thus, a single bout of IH confers a delayed EF benefit across low- to high-fit individuals, potentially reflecting multiple interacting (neuro)physiological changes.

articles.title: Dynamic responsivity of heart rate variability metrics to changing exercise intensity.
articles.authors: Matias Kanniainen, Johannes Mämmelä, Agnese Sbrollini et al.
articles.abstract: Heart rate variability (HRV) provides a non-invasive measure of autonomic regulation during exercise. Here, we examine the dynamic responsiveness of conventional and non-linear HRV metrics, with particular focus on dynamical detrended fluctuation analysis (DDFA), to changes in running intensity. Ten healthy runners completed a multi-phase outdoor protocol comprising flat, uphill, downhill and recovery segments, with RR intervals recorded via chest-worn ECG. HRV indices included RMSSD, SDRR, LF/HF, SD1/SD2, DFA α1 and the DDFA exponent α ∼ ( t ) . Phase-averaged non-linear metrics showed very strong Spearman correlations (|ρ| = 0.99, P = 0.000309) with a phase-dependent intensity index, Ik. DFA α1 and SDRR showed strong correlations (|ρ| = 0.93, P = 0.00767), LF/HF moderate non-significant association (|ρ| = 0.70, P = 0.125), and RMSSD virtually none (|ρ| = 0.06, P = 0.913). Time-lagged windowed cross-correlation analysis revealed that conventional metrics lost coupling with heart rate during sustained exertion, whereas SD1/SD2, DFA α1 and, especially, DDFA α ∼ ( t ) maintained clear intensity-dependent modulation. During recovery, DDFA α ∼ ( t ) returned rapidly towards baseline, consistent with parasympathetic reactivation. DDFA more effectively tracks rapid changes in exercise intensity than conventional HRV measures.

articles.title: Does succinic acid treatment improve metabolic health in a male murine model of early ageing?
articles.authors: Stephen J Ives, Kendall S Zaleski, Cheyanne Slocum et al.
articles.abstract: Ageing associates with obesity, mitochondrial dysfunction, and impaired glucose homeostasis. Previously, we documented that succinic acid (SA) treatment improves mitochondrial function and adiposity; however, the effects on ageing are unknown. Therefore, we determined the effect of SA treatment on metabolic health in 19 aged male mice (Age; 16 months), randomized to receive vehicle (Veh, n = 8) or SA (n = 11) and compared to young controls (Young; 6 months) (n = 24). After 6 weeks of treatment, insulin tolerance (IT), glucose tolerance (GT), pyruvate tolerance (PT) and physical activity (PA) were assessed. Body mass (BM), epididymal white adipose tissue (EWAT) and heart mass (HM) were measured at study end. Soleus muscle and EWAT underwent mitochondrial respirometry. Mice in the Age group had higher HM and EWAT (both P < 0.001). Blood glucose levels were higher in the Age group during the PT test (25470 ± 1206 vs. 31884 ± 4348 area under the curve (AUC), P = 0.014, Young vs. Age, respectively), though GT and IT were not affected (P > 0.05). PA was ∼50% lower in the Age group (8778 ± 5774 vs. 4132 ± 1523 rev/day), though Age-SA had 48% higher PA (Age-SA 6118 ± 2203 rev/day). SA treatment did not affect BM (37.8 ± 2.7 vs. 37.7 ± 3.2 g), EWAT (1.4 ± 0.4 vs. 1.3 ± 0.4 g) or HM (0.17 ± 0.01 vs. 0.19 ± 0.04 g, Age-Veh vs. Age-SA, all P > 0.05, respectively). GT AUC differed by group (P = 0.019), with Age-SA having lower AUC (Young 47120 ± 8751 vs. Age-SA 37180 ± 5383 AUC, P < 0.018), but not IT or PT (both P > 0.22). SA reversed the age-associated reduction in complex I+II-driven respiration in adipose (P < 0.05). Ageing elevated adiposity, impaired pyruvate tolerance and reduced adipose mitochondrial function, though SA was partially restorative in mitigating these age-associated effects, warranting further study.

articles.title: Identifying Players' Performance Profiles in Elite Men and Women 3 × 3 Basketball: Evidence From the Olympic Games.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Shaoliang Zhang, Lorenzo Gasperi, Miguel-Angel Gomez-Ruano et al.
articles.abstract: Zhang, S, Gasperi, L, Gomez-Ruano, M-A, Conte, D, and Sansone, P. Identifying player's performance profiles in elite men and women 3×3 basketball: Evidence from the Olympic Games. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to cluster the performance profiles of elite male and female 3 × 3 basketball players according to their stature. Data from the 2021 and 2024 Olympic Games were retrieved, involving 128 players (64 per sex). The players' stature was noted, alongside the game-related statistics (GRS) for all tournament games. Two-step cluster analyses classified male and female players according to their stature, whereas comparisons of GRS across clusters were performed using independent samples t test, Mann-Whitney U test, or 1-way ANOVA. For men, 2 clusters were identified: perimeter and internal. The analyses of performance profiles showed how perimeter players registered more 2-point shots made, 2-point shots attempted, key assists, and drives than internal players (all p < 0.05, effect size [ES]: small-moderate), whereas internal players had more 1-point shots made, 1-point shots attempted, free-throws attempted, and blocked shots than perimeter players (all p < 0.05, ES: small-moderate). For women, 3 clusters were identified: perimeter, all around, and internal. Perimeter players achieved more 2-point shots made, 2-point shots attempted, and drives than internal players (all p < 0.05, ES: moderate-large). All-around players only differed from internal players in their lower 1-point shots attempted (p = 0.043, ES: moderate). Internal players recorded more 1-point shots made than both perimeter and all-around players (all p < 0.05, ES: moderate) and more defensive rebounds than perimeter players (p = 0.010, ES: moderate). Current results provide initial information on the positional performance profile of elite male and female 3 × 3 basketball players, which can inform player selection, talent identification, strength and conditioning practices, and technical-tactical strategies.

articles.title: Effect of Interrepetition Rest Set Structures on Total Volume, Velocity Loss, and Rating of Perceived Exertion Accuracy.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Caitlyn M Meehan, Timothy B Davies, Jake A Ridenoure et al.
articles.abstract: Meehan, CM, Davies, TB, Ridenoure, JA, Gotla, TX, Thompson, BK, Walpole, KJ, Watson, BA, and Colquhoun, RJ. Effect of interrepetition rest set structures on total volume, velocity loss, and rating of perceived exertion accuracy. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The purpose of this study was to examine differences between traditional sets (TS) and 2 different interrepetition rest (IRR) set structures on the amount of volume able to be performed, velocity loss (VL), and rating of perceived exertion (RPE) accuracy across sets to a fixed RPE in the back squat. Twenty (10 males and 10 females) healthy, resistance-trained subjects reported to the laboratory for a 1 repetition maximum visit and 3 experimental visits in the back squat, where subjects were randomized into a different protocol for each visit. The 3 experimental visits consisted of a set to an 8 and 10+ RPE in the following conditions: (a) TS that involved 0 seconds of intraset rest and 180 seconds of interset rest (TS); (b) IRR that involved 40 seconds of intraset rest and 180 seconds of interset rest (IRR-180); and (c) IRR that involved 40 seconds of intraset rest and 40 seconds of interset rest (IRR-40). Our results indicate that the number of repetitions completed was significantly greater in IRR-180 and IRR-40 when compared with TS (p < 0.001-0.030). In addition, despite greater volume completed in IRR-180 and IRR-40, VL was significantly lower in these conditions (-17.7% ± 4.6% and -18.1% ± 4.5%, respectively) when compared with TS (-24.7 ± 8.6%; p = 0.019). Finally, RPE accuracy was significantly greater in TS when compared with both IRR-180 and IRR-40 (p < 0.001). The present data suggest that IRR set structures allow for additional volume to be performed compared with TS when exertion is held constant, without increasing mechanical fatigue.

articles.title: Biomechanical, Anthropometric, Body Composition, Psychological, and Training-Related Correlates of Barbell Deadlift Strength.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Adam E Mohan, Alec Piñero, Dan Montenegro et al.
articles.abstract: Mohan, AE, Piñero, A, Montenegro, D, Rivera, O, Van Every, DW, Larsen, S, Androulakis Korakakis, P, Swinton, PA, and Schoenfeld, BJ. Biomechanical, anthropometric, body composition, psychological, and training-related correlates of barbell deadlift strength. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-To examine the relative contributions of biomechanical, body composition, anthropometric, psychological, and training-related variables to maximal barbell deadlift strength in resistance-trained individuals, 21 well-trained subjects (17 men, 4 women) completed assessments of body composition, anthropometry, motion capture, isometric dynamometry, psychological characteristics, and 1 repetition maximum (1RM) deadlift performance. Given the number of candidate predictors relative to the sample size, analyses were framed as theory-informed and exploratory rather than tests of causal determinants. Bayesian correlation and regression analyses, including bootstrap LASSO and Bayesian grouped-shrinkage models, were used to identify variables associated with deadlift strength. Body composition variables demonstrated the strongest associations with deadlift 1RM, particularly fat-free mass and lean mass. After adjustment for height and body mass, lean mass retained positive associations with performance, whereas fat mass showed negative associations. Relative arm length was also positively associated with deadlift strength. Bootstrap LASSO analyses identified arm lean mass as the most consistently retained predictor (67% of models), followed by isometric knee net joint moment (54%). Neck circumference, ankle width, and handgrip strength showed weaker and less consistent associations. In the Bayesian grouped-shrinkage model, body composition exhibited the strongest domain-level signal (τ = 0.31, 95% CrI: 0.08-0.92) and the highest probability of being the most influential predictor domain (0.53), exceeding anthropometric, biomechanical, training, psychological, and demographic domains. Body size and body composition, particularly lean mass, appear to provide the strongest and most consistent signal for maximal deadlift performance, whereas psychological characteristics contribute comparatively little in resistance-trained individuals.

articles.title: Effects of Moderate Weight Loss on the Thermic Effect of Food and Postprandial Substrate Oxidation in Healthy Normal-Weight Adults.
articles.journal: Applied physiology, nutrition, and metabolism = Physiologie appliquee, nutrition et metabolisme
articles.authors: Noémie Beauregard, Léna Pélissier, Ines Ramos et al.
articles.abstract: While most weight-loss research focuses on individuals with obesity, normal-weight individuals also frequently attempt to lose weight through dietary restriction. However, the effects of weight loss on the thermic effect of food, a less well-studied component of total energy expenditure, remain poorly documented in this population. Normal-weight adults (age = 23.3 ± 3.8 years, BMI = 22.8 ± 1.9 kg.m-2) achieved 3% (n = 32, 23 females) and 6% (n = 18, 11 females) reductions in initial body weight. Postprandial energy expenditure and substrate oxidation were assessed following consumption of a standardized breakfast. Compared with baseline, TEF slightly increased after 3% weight loss (β = 0.05 kcal·min⁻¹, 95% CI 0.018-0.084; p = 0.002) but did not differ from baseline after 6% weight loss. Total postprandial fat oxidation increased at both 3% and 6% weight loss compared with baseline, whereas total carbohydrate oxidation decreased at both time points. Future studies should determine whether larger magnitudes of weight loss, longer-term energy restriction, or weight loss achieved through increased energy expenditure, elicit changes in TEF and how such changes may influence long-term energy balance.

articles.title: 24-hour Movement Guideline Adherence and Cardiometabolic Health among Adults with Disabilities: Analysis of NHANES 2013-2018.
articles.journal: Applied physiology, nutrition, and metabolism = Physiologie appliquee, nutrition et metabolisme
articles.authors: Yahan Liang, Xihe Zhu, Justin Haegele
articles.abstract: A growing body of evidence has examined the association between adherence to the 24-hour movement guidelines and cardiometabolic health outcomes. However, it remains unclear whether these associations extend to adults with disabilities, a population experiencing substantial health disparities. Therefore, this study examined the association between adherence to the 24-hour movement guidelines and cardiometabolic health among adults with disabilities. This cross-sectional study used data from the 2013-2018 cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES). A nationally representative sample of U.S. adults with disabilities (n = 4,985) was included. Survey-weighted logistic regression models with multiple imputation were used to examine associations between guideline adherence and cardiometabolic health. Subgroup analyses were conducted across cardiometabolic outcomes and functional disability types. The results showed that participants meeting three guidelines had higher odds of being free from cardiovascular disease (AOR = 2.05, 95% CI: 1.42-2.94), obesity (AOR = 1.99, 95% CI: 1.44-2.75), hypertension (AOR = 1.75, 95% CI: 1.22-2.50) and type 2 diabetes (AOR = 1.60, 95% CI: 1.14-2.24), than those meeting none of the guidelines. Meeting two guidelines was associated with higher odds of being free from hypertension and obesity. Associations between guideline adherence and cardiometabolic health varied across functional disability subgroups. These findings suggest that adherence to a greater number of movement guidelines is associated with having more favorable cardiometabolic health profiles for adults with disabilities. Exploratory subgroup analyses showed variation in the associations across disability types, further research is needed to determine whether associations differ across functional impairment groups and whether movement recommendations should be tailored accordingly.

articles.title: Recombinant type III collagen: a promising ingredient for enhancing skin repair post UVB exposure.
articles.authors: Qian Wang, Guodong Li, Fei Liu et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Skin damage is accelerated by UVB exposures. Therefore, it is essential to develop skin repair ingredients to protect the skin from damage caused by UVB exposures. This study was performed to evaluate the efficacy of recombinant type III collagen (RC-III) in alleviating damage induced by UVB exposure, and to elucidate its underlying mechanisms, using the normal human epidermal keratinocytes (NHEKs) and 3D epidermal models (EpiKutis®). METHODS: The MTT assay and cell morphology observations were used to assess the cytotoxicity of RC-III. The skin repair potential of RC-III was evaluated on NHEKs and EpiKutis® models by immunofluorescence (IF) staining, Reverse Transcription Quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR), enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), wound closure assay and ultra-high performance liquid chromatography-mass spectrometer (UHPLC-MS/MS). RESULTS: RC‑III showed no cytotoxicity against NHEKs at a concentration of 2 mg/mL. In the UVB‑damaged models, RC‑III displayed prominent antioxidant effect and anti‑inflammatory property while also modulating the expression of barrier‑related proteins and lipids. Specifically, RC-III could reduce the levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS), increase superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity, decrease the gene and protein expression of inflammatory factors and reduce the protein expression of NF-κB p65, promote the protein expression of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARα) and its downstream proteins, and restore the levels of skin lipids. CONCLUSIONS: All findings reported here are derived exclusively from in vitro systems. RC-III showed remarkable skin repair potential, effectively alleviating damage induced by UVB exposure in NHEKs and EpiKutis® models. Our study provided more scientific evidence for the application of RC-III.

articles.title: Carbohydrate quality and progression trajectories of cardiometabolic multimorbidity: a prospective cohort study with multi-omics analyses.
articles.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
articles.authors: Mingrui Chen, Huan Liu, Chenhui Zhang et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Carbohydrate quality is associated with cardiometabolic health, but its relationships with cardiometabolic multimorbidity (CMM) progression and molecular and genetic characteristics remain unclear. OBJECTIVE: To investigate associations of carbohydrate quality with CMM progression and explore potential multi-omics signatures, pathways, and genetic effect modification. METHODS: We included 177,763 UK Biobank participants free of baseline cardiometabolic diseases (CMDs). Carbohydrate quality was assessed using correlation and principal component analyses. Multivariable Cox and multi-state models evaluated CMD incidence and CMM progression. Carbohydrate-associated proteomic and metabolomic signatures were derived for exploratory mediation analyses, and genomic data were used for gene-environment-wide interaction study (GEWIS). RESULTS: During a median 12.56-year follow-up, 37,527, 5,751, and 650 participants developed first, double, and triple CMDs, respectively. High- and low-quality carbohydrates showed opposing associations with CMM accumulation, strongest for ≥3 CMDs [HRs (95% CIs): 0.92 (0.86, 0.98) and 1.11 (1.05, 1.19), respectively]. In multi-state analyses, associations were particularly evident for progression from hypertension to comorbid T2D [HRs (95% CIs): 0.98 (0.96, 0.99) and 1.05 (1.03, 1.06), respectively]. Exploratory multi-omics mediation analyses yielded statistical mediation signals, with estimated pathway-level mediation proportions for T2D of 40.1% for PPAR signalling with high-quality carbohydrates and 36.2% and 36.4% for PI3K-Akt and MAPK signalling with low-quality carbohydrates. GEWIS identified candidate interaction loci with genotype-dependent differences in carbohydrate-CMD associations. High-quality carbohydrates were inversely associated with CHD onset among rs17589271 TT carriers but positively associated among GT/GG carriers [HRs (95% CIs): 0.95 (0.93, 0.98) and 1.22 (1.10, 1.35), respectively]. Low-quality carbohydrates showed a stronger association with progression from prior CMDs to comorbid T2D among rs144465069 AG/AA carriers [HR (95% CI): 2.09 (1.57, 2.78)]. CONCLUSIONS: Carbohydrate quality was differentially associated with CMM progression. Exploratory multi-omics and genetic analyses highlighted potential pathways and genotype-specific associations. These findings may inform future research on personalised nutritional strategies for cardiometabolic prevention.

articles.title: Watermelon supplementation lowers blood pressure: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
articles.authors: Yunzhen Lei, Jiaying Diao, Ming Xu et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Watermelon contains L-citrulline, polyphenols, lycopene, and other bioactive compounds that may influence vascular function and blood pressure regulation. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the effects of watermelon supplementation on blood pressure, arterial stiffness-related indices, autonomic function, lipid metabolism, and anthropometric parameters. METHODS: PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to May 13, 2026. Randomized controlled trials comparing watermelon, watermelon juice, or watermelon extract with non-watermelon control interventions were included. Methodological quality was assessed using the revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool, and evidence certainty was evaluated using the GRADE framework. Continuous outcomes were synthesized using mean differences with 95% confidence intervals. Crossover trials were analyzed as paired data, with each participant counted once; when paired variance information was unavailable, a within-participant correlation coefficient of 0.50 was assumed. Primary analyses used post-intervention values, and analyses based on change-from-baseline values were conducted as supplementary analyses. Heterogeneity was explored using subgroup analysis, meta-regression, restricted cubic spline analysis, and leave-one-out sensitivity analysis. Trial sequential analysis was conducted using unique participant counts. RESULTS: Sixteen randomized controlled trials were included. Five trials were judged to have a low risk of bias, eight had some concerns, and three had a high risk of bias. In the post-intervention primary analysis, watermelon supplementation was associated with lower systolic blood pressure (SBP; 12 studies; WMD, -5.53 mmHg; 95% CI, -8.99 to -2.06; P=0.002; I2=89.7%) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP; 12 studies; WMD, -2.55 mmHg; 95% CI, -3.77 to -1.33; P<0.001; I2=57.1%). Significant pooled reductions were observed for first systolic peak pressure and pulse pressure, whereas second systolic peak pressure, mean arterial pressure, reflection time, heart rate, pulse-wave velocity, augmentation index, and anthropometric and lipid outcomes were not statistically significant. Among autonomic outcomes, RMSSD and high-frequency power increased, whereas SDNN, low-frequency power, and the LF/HF ratio did not show statistically significant changes; these outcomes were each informed by two studies. Exploratory subgroup and study-level meta-regression analyses showed nominal differences across study characteristics, but these analyses were based on sparse, potentially confounded evidence and were not adjusted for multiple comparisons. Restricted cubic spline analyses found no evidence of nonlinearity. In the TSA analysis, 236 unique participants represented 15.9% and 28.9% of the required information sizes for SBP and DBP, respectively, and neither cumulative Z-curve crossed the trial sequential monitoring boundary. Potential small-study effects could not be excluded. According to the current GRADE profile, certainty was very low for SBP and low for DBP. CONCLUSIONS: Watermelon supplementation was associated with lower SBP and DBP, but substantial heterogeneity, limited accrued information, and low certainty of evidence restrict confidence in the estimated effects. Evidence for haemodynamic, autonomic, arterial-stiffness, lipid, and anthropometric outcomes was inconsistent and was usually based on few studies. The subgroup and meta-regression findings are exploratory study-level observations and do not establish patient-level effect modification or an optimal intervention regimen. Larger, well-designed randomized controlled trials with prespecified analyses are needed.
